results.name: common_factor_rule_gap
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share a greatest common divisor g>=3, yes rate for targets divisible by g minus yes rate for targets not divisible by g; observed > model means people generalize the shared "multiples of g" rule more sharply than graded-factor coherence-tuned similarity predicts (tracks whether the iter-3 refinement closed this gap).
results.code:
# name: common_factor_rule_gap
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share a greatest common divisor g>=3, yes rate for targets divisible by g minus yes rate for targets not divisible by g; observed > model means people generalize the shared "multiples of g" rule more sharply than graded-factor coherence-tuned similarity predicts (tracks whether the iter-3 refinement closed this gap).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = s.unique()
    gmap = {}
    for u in uniq:
        v = [int(z) for z in u.split(",")]
        g = 0
        for z in v:
            g = math.gcd(g, z)
        gmap[u] = g if (len(v) >= 2 and g >= 3) else 0
    g = s.map(gmap).values.astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    m = g > 0
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    div = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    div[m] = (t[m] % g[m]) == 0
    a = m & div
    b = m & ~div
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; observed > model (model ~0, being stationary) means yes responses become more frequent later in the session.

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across number sets of each set's mean yes rate; observed > model means people treat some sets as far more (or less) generous than the model, i.e. the model under-produces set-level extremity (near-all-yes / near-all-no sets).

results.name: large_vs_small_far_target_gap
results.description: Among targets more than 20 away from every example, yes rate for targets > 50 minus yes rate for targets <= 50; observed != model means people carry a target-magnitude bias the similarity model lacks (observed > model: they over-endorse large far targets; observed < model: they over-endorse small far targets).
results.code:
# name: large_vs_small_far_target_gap
# description: Among targets more than 20 away from every example, yes rate for targets > 50 minus yes rate for targets <= 50; observed != model means people carry a target-magnitude bias the similarity model lacks (observed > model: they over-endorse large far targets; observed < model: they over-endorse small far targets).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4))
    E = ex.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    mind = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    far = mind > 20
    a = far & (t > 50)
    b = far & (t <= 50)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: single_example_distance_gradient
results.description: In 1-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example itself) minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed > model means people generalize from a lone example with a steeper magnitude gradient than the model's noisy baseline-gain similarity predicts (observed < model means a flatter gradient).
results.code:
# name: single_example_distance_gradient
# description: In 1-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example itself) minus yes rate for targets more than 30 away; observed > model means people generalize from a lone example with a steeper magnitude gradient than the model's noisy baseline-gain similarity predicts (observed < model means a flatter gradient).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    sm = single.values
    dd = np.abs(t - x)
    a = sm & (dd >= 1) & (dd <= 10)
    b = sm & (dd > 30)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: far_target_size_principle
results.description: Yes rate for targets more than 30 away from every example in 3-4-example sets minus the same far-target yes rate in 1-example sets; observed < model means people tighten generalization with more examples (size principle) more than the averaged exemplar similarity predicts, observed > model means they broaden it more.
results.code:
# name: far_target_size_principle
# description: Yes rate for targets more than 30 away from every example in 3-4-example sets minus the same far-target yes rate in 1-example sets; observed < model means people tighten generalization with more examples (size principle) more than the averaged exemplar similarity predicts, observed > model means they broaden it more.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4))
    E = ex.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    dist = np.abs(E - t[:, None])
    mind = np.nanmin(dist, axis=1)
    far = mind > 30
    a = far & (k >= 3)
    b = far & (k == 1)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: item_extremity_incoherent_sets
results.description: Among (set, target) items from single-example or low-coherence sets (mean pairwise coherence over size/digit/parity/shared-factor < 0.4), the fraction of items whose yes rate is <= 1/9 or >= 8/9; observed > model means people answer decisively even after incoherent sets, contrary to the model's baseline-noisy decision rule there (observed < model means they are noisier than predicted).
results.code:
# name: item_extremity_incoherent_sets
# description: Among (set, target) items from single-example or low-coherence sets (mean pairwise coherence over size/digit/parity/shared-factor < 0.4), the fraction of items whose yes rate is <= 1/9 or >= 8/9; observed > model means people answer decisively even after incoherent sets, contrary to the model's baseline-noisy decision rule there (observed < model means they are noisier than predicted).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    cmap = {}
    for u in s.unique():
        v = [int(z) for z in u.split(",")]
        pr = [(v[i], v[j]) for i in range(len(v)) for j in range(i + 1, len(v))]
        if not pr:
            cmap[u] = 0.0
            continue
        def fm(a, b):
            m = min(a, b)
            return 0.0 if m <= 1 else 1.0 - math.log(math.gcd(a, b)) / math.log(m)
        c0 = np.mean([max(0.0, 1 - abs(a - b) / 50.0) for a, b in pr])
        c1 = np.mean([a % 10 == b % 10 for a, b in pr])
        c2 = np.mean([a % 2 == b % 2 for a, b in pr])
        c3 = np.mean([1 - fm(a, b) for a, b in pr])
        cmap[u] = float((c0 + c1 + c2 + c3) / 4.0)
    coh = s.map(cmap).values
    d = pd.DataFrame({"s": s.values, "t": df["target"].astype(int).values,
                      "y": df["rating"].astype(float).values})
    d = d[coh < 0.4]
    if len(d) == 0:
        return 0.0
    m = d.groupby(["s", "t"])["y"].mean().values
    return float(np.mean((m <= 1.0 / 9 + 1e-9) | (m >= 8.0 / 9 - 1e-9)))

results.name: shared_final_digit_rule_gap
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all end in the same digit, yes rate for targets with that final digit minus yes rate for other targets; observed > model means people apply an "ends in d" rule more sharply than coherence-stretched digit attention predicts (observed < model means the model over-weights digit coherence).
results.code:
# name: shared_final_digit_rule_gap
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all end in the same digit, yes rate for targets with that final digit minus yes rate for other targets; observed > model means people apply an "ends in d" rule more sharply than coherence-stretched digit attention predicts (observed < model means the model over-weights digit coherence).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    dmap = {}
    for u in s.unique():
        v = [int(z) for z in u.split(",")]
        ds = set(z % 10 for z in v)
        dmap[u] = ds.pop() if (len(v) >= 2 and len(ds) == 1) else -1
    d = s.map(dmap).values.astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    m = d >= 0
    a = m & (t % 10 == d)
    b = m & (t % 10 != d)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
